title: Winning a spot on the Fitch Bandwagon national radio show, 1942
summary: With Basie's arrangements and his wife's help collecting ballots, the band is picked to represent St. Louis on the Fitch program from the Kiel Opera House and gets telegrams from across the country.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: 1942, -- anyway, 1942 was a good year for the band, personnel-wise. And it was good from the music standpoint because Count Basie had been through here and had given us several beautiful scores by Hugo Winterhalter, Buster Harding, and several other arrangers. And this helped our repertoire. We kept rehearsing the band, and we tried to inject some original ideas into these various arrangements that we had.

In the meantime, there was a program on every Sunday afternoon called the Fitz Bandwagon program. And they would advertise from various cities throughout America, the most popular band in that territory. So we decided to get in the contest. There was a drug company in St. Louis called Meyers Drug Company. They were the key people in the city of St. Louis representing NBC and the agency -- advertising agency who had the account for the Fitz Bandwagon people.

I went down and talked with Mr. Meyers. He was living then. And he told me that all I had to do was get the votes out in different establishments and when they're tallied, the top score would go to the winner. So I got out -- I was married then, and my wife and I, we drove around, over to on Selto and different places in St. Louis, and put these little boxes up, put our names up and asked people to sign our names to it. All over town we did it. Asked the different fellows in the band to do the same thing. Which they did, they helped out.

Finally, I got a letter from Chicago. Evidently this gentleman worked for the advertising agency who was handling the account. And he told me that our band had been one of the bands selected to represent St. Louis. So instead of picking one band, they had picked two bands. They picked a white band and a black band. I can't think of the white band's name. Can you think of their name, Charles?
No, I can't think of the name either. (Unaudible)

He had a small combo. He had about a six-piece band. We had a big band. So the gentleman wrote me and told me they would have a from New York representatives to come out from New York to St. Louis and explain the entire program to us. And which the gentleman did come. I do remember his name. His last name was Barron. We met with Mr. Barron, and Mr. Barron allocated X number of tunes for us, X number of tunes for the other band.

And we had to rehearse and refine the timing of the various tunes that we played to so many minutes. This we did. And on that Sunday afternoon, we appeared at the Opera House of the Kiel Auditorium, which was packed and jammed. The main announcer of the show -- his name was Toby Reed.
We got down earlier, and we tuned up real good. And

we rehearsed our part of the program. And it came out right on the second. The other band did the same, it came out. There was some announcements being made between each tunes -- each tune, rather, featuring the Fitz shampoo.

We started the program off with our theme song, and the band opened up with a fast tune. I think the name of that tune was "Sleep." But the band was in good shape, they played in tune, and they sounded beautiful to me because I was directing the band and I was out front. That evening, after we got through playing, we got telegrams from California, from Boston, we got about ten telegrams from people who had heard the program, admired the band. We got telegrams from one or two booking agents. And everybody was happy about the whole thing. It was a great experience for the band, and a great experience to my partner, Jeter, and myself, because we had never appeared before on a national hookup.

Many people talked about that show that we played. Many weeks and month later, friends from Cleveland, Ohio called up and wrote letters, telling us about the program. '42 -- the summer of '42 was good and kind to us.
